messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 0.76 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal (weak); Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 6800 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weakest excitation; Ip = 8 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 10 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       0.56   0.566    11.6       -    0.0314  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S2      0.558   0.563    11.2       -    0.0457  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       2.24    2.26    35.4   0.329     0.228  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S4      0.334   0.339    8.95       -   0.00508  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S5      0.573   0.581    15.7       -    0.0329  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6      0.459   0.462     6.1       -    0.0211  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out,min} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (settled mean)
        *   $V_{out,max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (cold start)
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (settled stability)
    *   Piezo Model: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25-30 nF) and $R_{leak} = 20\text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   Operating Conditions:
        *   S1: Nominal ($I_p=12\mu\text{A}$, $f=100\text{Hz}$, $R_L=10\text{M}\Omega$)
        *   S2: Heavy load ($R_L=6.8\text{M}\Omega$)
        *   S3: Strong excitation, light load ($I_p=40\mu\text{A}$, $R_L=22\text{M}\Omega$)
        *   S4: Weakest excitation ($I_p=8\mu\text{A}$, $R_L=22\text{M}\Omega$)
        *   S5: Low frequency ($f=80\text{Hz}$, $I_p=10\mu\text{A}$, $R_L=10\text{M}\Omega$)
        *   S6: $C_p$ increase, Hot ($C_p=30\text{nF}$, $I_p=12\mu\text{A}$, $R_L=10\text{M}\Omega$)
    *   Reference FBR (Full-Bridge Rectifier) failed on $V_{out,min}$ and $t_{up}$ because the open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} = \frac{I_p}{2\pi f C_p} \approx 0.76\text{ V}$ is far below the required 1.8 V.

    *   The source voltage is too low for a simple rectifier. A voltage boost is needed.
    *   Since $V_{oc}$ is very low (around 0.76 V), a passive rectifier cannot reach 1.8 V unless the load is extremely light and the charging time is very long (but we have a $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ constraint).
    *   We need a DC-DC converter. Specifically, an SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) or a similar switched-capacitor/inductor technique to flip the voltage across $C_p$ and effectively "pump" the charge.
    *   Standard SSHI logic:
        1.  Piezo charges $C_p$.
        2.  At peak voltage, a switch closes to invert the voltage across $C_p$ using an inductor $L$.
        3.  The inverted voltage adds to the piezo's generated voltage, increasing the effective voltage across the rectifier.

    *   *Approach 1: Standard SSHI (Inverter + Rectifier).*
        *   Use a SYNC controller to flip the piezo voltage at both peaks.
        *   Inductor $L$ in parallel with $C_p$ (via switch).
        *   Rectifier (bridge or half-bridge) to extract energy to $C_{out}$.
        *   Wait, the standard SSHI flips $C_p$ voltage, which increases the voltage seen by the rectifier. If we can pump the voltage high enough, a rectifier can then charge $C_{out}$ to 1.8 V.

    *   *Approach 2: Synchronous Boost/Charge Pump.*
        *   Since $V_{oc}$ is low, we need a way to accumulate charge and step it up.
        *   A simple SSHI setup:
            *   Piezo nodes: `pzp`, `pzn`.
            *   Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ used for inversion.
            *   Rectifier diodes to $V_{out}$.
            *   Wait, the most efficient way to get $V_{out} > V_{oc}$ is to utilize the resonance between $L$ and $C_p$.

    *   *Refining SSHI Topology:*
        *   Piezo is between `pzp` and `pzn`.
        *   Inversion circuit: $L$ connects `pzp` to a node `n1`, and a switch $S$ connects `n1` to `pzn`.
        *   Rectification: To get power to `out`, we need diodes. A simple diode from `pzp` to `out` and `pzn` to `out` (half-bridge) or a full-bridge.
        *   Let's try a half-bridge with the SSHI inversion.
        *   $L$ and $S$ are used to flip the voltage on $C_p$.
        *   When $V_{pzp} - V_{pzn}$ is at a peak, $S$ closes, $L$ oscillates with $C_p$, and the voltage is inverted.

    *   *Calculation for $L$:*
        $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
        If $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$ and we want $t_{on} \approx 50\mu\text{s}$, $L \approx \frac{(50\mu\text{s})^2}{\pi^2 \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx 10\text{ mH}$. (Max $L$ is $0.01\text{ H} = 10\text{ mH}$).

    *   *Topology Proposal 1: SSHI with Half-Bridge*
        - $L1$: `pzp` to `n1`
        - $S1$: `n1` to `pzn` (Ctrl: $G1$)
        - $G1$: `edges`: `both`, `phase`: 0.0 (hits peaks)
        - $D1$: `pzp` to `out` (DSCH)
        - $D2$: `pzn` to `out` (Wait, this is wrong. For a half-bridge, $pzn$ must be ground or we need a full bridge).
        - Let's use a Full Bridge Rectifier (FBR) + SSHI.
        - Full Bridge:
            - $D1$: `pzp` $\to$ `out`
            - $D2$: `pzn` $\to$ `out`
            - $D3$: `0` $\to$ `pzp`
            - $D4$: `0` $\to$ `pzn`
            - (Wait, the problem states the return diodes have their anode on ground: `["0", "pzp"]` and `["0", "pzn"]`).
        - SSHI part:
            - $L1$: `pzp` $\to$ `n1`
            - $S1$: `n1` $\to$ `pzn`
            - $G1$: `edges`: `both`, `ton`: $\pi \sqrt{LC_p}$.

    *   *Topology Proposal 2: SSHI with modified inversion.*
        Maybe a simpler diode-capacitor multiplier or a specific boost structure? No, SSHI is the gold standard for low $V_{oc}$ piezo.

    *   *Topology Proposal 3: Synchronous Charge Pump (if possible).*
        Actually, the SYNC controller is designed for this. Let's try a variant of the SSHI.

    *   *Checking the "Screening" condition:*
        The screening checks if the circuit delivers $>50\%$ of $V^2/R_L$ at $V=1.8\text{ V}$.
        $P_{load} = 1.8^2 / R_L$. For S2 ($R_L=6.8\text{M}\Omega$), $P \approx 0.47\mu\text{W}$.
        The energy harvested per cycle in SSHI is significantly higher than in FBR. FBR just takes the current; SSHI flips the voltage to keep the current flowing in the same direction into the load.

    *   *Constraint check: $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$.*
        Need a zener clamp `DZ33` on `out` to ensure it doesn't exceed 3.6 V (though 3.3 V is the zener voltage).

    *   *Detailed Component List for Proposal 1 (SSHI + FBR):*
        - $D1$: `pzp` $\to$ `out` (DSCH)
        - $D2$: `pzn` $\to$ `out` (DSCH)
        - $D3$: `0` $\to$ `pzp` (DSCH)
        - $D4$: `0` $\to$ `pzn` (DSCH)
        - $L1$: `pzp` $\to$ `n1` (Value: e.g., $4.7\text{ mH}$)
        - $S1$: `n1` $\to$ `pzn` (Ctrl: `G1`)
        - $G1$: `edges`: `both`, `ton`: $3.4\text{e-05}$ ($\pi \sqrt{4.7\text{mH} \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx 34\mu\text{s}$)
        - $C_{out}$: `out` $\to$ `0` (Value: $2.2\mu\text{F}$)
        - $D_{zener}$: `0` $\to$ `out` (DZ33)

    *   *Wait, check the Full Bridge rectifier logic:*
        In the reference FBR:
        $D1$: `pzp` $\to$ `out`
        $D2$: `pzn` $\to$ `out`
        $D3$: `0` $\to$ `pzp`
        $D4$: `0` $\to$ `pzn`
        Is this a standard bridge?
        If $pzp > pzn$ and $pzp > 0, pzn > 0$, then $D1$ conducts.
        If $pzp < pzn$ and $pzp < 0, pzn < 0$, then $D2$ conducts.
        Yes, it's a bridge. $D3$ and $D4$ are the return paths to ground.

    *   *Alternative Proposal (Parallel SSHI):*
        Some SSHI designs use a switch to short $C_p$ or use a different inductor placement. The $L$-$S$ branch in parallel with the piezo is the most common.

    *   *Wait, let's consider the "cold start" $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$.*
        SSHI is much faster than FBR because it increases the voltage amplitude.

    *   *Looking at the components limit (16):*
        Our current list: 4 diodes (bridge) + 1 zener + 1 inductor + 1 switch + 1 sync + 1 capacitor = 9 components. This is well within the limit.

    *   *Is there a more efficient way?*
        Maybe an SSHI that only flips on one edge? No, `both` is usually better for power.

    *   *Let's double-check the $L$ value.*
        $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$. $L = 10\text{ mH} \implies T_{res} = 2\pi\sqrt{LC_p} \approx 100\mu\text{s}$.
        $t_{on}$ should be half a period for a full flip: $\pi\sqrt{LC_p} \approx 50\mu\text{s}$.
        If $L = 4.7\text{ mH}$, $t_{on} \approx 34\mu\text{s}$.

    *   *Consider the return path again:*
        The reference FBR used: `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`.
        Let's stick to that.

    *   *Let's propose 2 variations of the SSHI.*
        One with $L$ in the flipping branch and one with a different configuration.
        Wait, the prompt allows 3 proposals.

    *   *Proposal 1: Classic SSHI + Full Bridge + Zener.*
        - $L1$ from `pzp` to `n1`.
        - $S1$ from `n1` to `pzn`.
        - $G1$ (SYNC) controlling $S1$, `edges: both`, `ton: 34us`.
        - Bridge: `pzp->out`, `pzn->out`, `0->pzp`, `0->pzn`.
        - $C_{out}$ on `out`.
        - Zener on `out`.

    *   *Proposal 2: SSHI with a switch to invert $C_p$ directly?*
        (No, you need the inductor to avoid current spikes and actually transfer the energy).

    *   *Proposal 3: SSHI using a different switching point (phase shift).*
        The SYNC is already flexible. Maybe try a design with only one diode to `out` (half-bridge) and a large $C_{out}$, but the piezo is AC, so we need to capture both halves.

    *   *Wait, let's reconsider the inversion.*
        In a standard SSHI, the switch $S$ is in parallel with $C_p$ and $L$.
        $C_p$ is between `pzp` and `pzn`.
        $L$ and $S$ should be in parallel with $C_p$.
        So: $L$ from `pzp` to `n1`, $S$ from `n1` to `pzn`. (This is what I had).
        Wait, $L$ and $S$ are in series, and that combination is in parallel with $C_p$.
        Correct.

    *   *Let's think about the $V_{oc}$ again.*
        $V_{oc} \approx 0.76\text{ V}$.
        FBR failed because $0.76\text{ V} < 1.8\text{ V} + 2 \times 0.25\text{ V}$.
        SSHI increases the voltage across $C_p$ to $V_{sshi} = V_{oc} \cdot \frac{1+ \gamma}{1 - \gamma}$ (roughly), where $\gamma$ is the inversion efficiency.
        If we can get the piezo voltage to $\sim 3\text{ V}$, then $3\text{ V} - 0.5\text{ V} = 2.5\text{ V}$ which can charge the capacitor to $1.8\text{ V}$.

    *   *What about $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$?*
        $C_{out} = 2.2\mu\text{F}$.
        Required charge $\Delta Q = 2.2\mu\text{F} \cdot 1.8\text{ V} \approx 4\mu\text{C}$.
        $I_p = 12\mu\text{A}$. Charge per half cycle $\approx I_p / (\pi f) \approx 12\mu\text{A} / 314 \approx 38\text{ nC}$.
        With SSHI, we might get more, but still, $4\mu\text{C} / 38\text{ nC} \approx 100$ cycles.
        At $100\text{ Hz}$, 100 cycles is $0.5\text{ s}$.
        This is close to the $0.4\text{ s}$ limit.
        We might need a smaller $C_{out}$ to start faster. Let's try $1\mu\text{F}$ or $0.47\mu\text{F}$?
        Wait, $C_{out}$ is optimized by the evolution strategy, so I just need to provide a reasonable starting value.

    *   *Refining Proposal 1:*
        - $C_{out}$: $1\mu\text{F}$
        - $L1$: $10\text{ mH}$
        - $t_{on}$: $\pi \sqrt{10\text{mH} \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx 50\mu\text{s}$.

    *   *Wait, is there any other topology?*
        Maybe a "synchronous rectifier" using switches instead of diodes?
        The problem says we have at most 4 switches.
        If we use switches for the bridge, we'd need 4 switches.
        But we also need the SSHI inversion switch. That's 5 switches. (Limit is 4).
        So we must use diodes for the rectifier.

    *   *Checking for a "cold start" issue:*
        SSHI requires the SYNC controller to work. The SYNC controller is "ideal" and "tracks the excitation frequency automatically", and its power cost is $0.5\mu\text{A}$ drawn from `out`. This means it can run even if `out` is low? The prompt says "supply current drawn from out", usually meaning it needs $V_{out} > 0$. But "ideal" often means it starts as soon as there's some voltage.

    *   *Let's refine the bridge.*
        The prompt suggests the FBR: `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`.
        Wait, if $pzp$ is positive and $pzn$ is negative, $D1$ (`pzp` $\to$ `out`) and $D3$ (`0` $\to$ `pzp`) would both be reverse-biased?
        No:
        If $pzp = 2\text{V}$, $pzn = -2\text{V}$:
        $D1$: $pzp(2) \to out(1.8)$. Conducts.
        $D4$: $0 \to pzn(-2)$. Conducts.
        So $D1$ and $D4$ conduct. This is a correct path.

    *   *Final Topology Choice:*
        Proposal 1: SSHI + Full Bridge + Zener.
        Proposal 2: SSHI + Half Bridge (simpler, but maybe less power).
        Actually, let's try the SSHI with different $L$ values or $t_{on}$ in the optimization, but the connectivity is the same. I'll propose a a few variations of SSHI if I can think of any.
        Wait, I can use a "capacitor-based" SSHI? No, that's more complex.
        Let's stick to the L-SSHI.

    *   *Wait!* There is another common SSHI variant where the inductor is not in series with the switch.
        But the $L$-series-S parallel to $C_p$ is the most common "SSHI" (specifically, the "Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor" or SECE - Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction).
        Actually, SECE is different. SECE uses an inductor and a switch to extract all the energy at the peak.
        SECE Topology:
        1. $C_p$ charges.
        2. At peak, $S1$ closes, connecting $C_p$ to $L$.
        3. $L$ and $C_p$ oscillate.
        4. At the peak of the $L$ current, $S2$ closes, connecting $L$ to the rectifier.
        This is more complex and requires two switches and precise timing.

        Let's stick to the basic SSHI (flipping the voltage).
        One more check on the "Half Bridge" (Proposal 2):
        If we use a half-bridge, we need $pzn$ to be ground. But $pzn$ is a piezo terminal.
        Wait, if we use the SSHI to flip $C_p$, and $C_p$ is between `pzp` and `pzn`, we can just use a diode from `pzp` to `out` and a diode from `pzn` to `out`... but we still need a return path.
        If we don't have a return path to ground, it won't work.
        If we use $D1$: `pzp` $\to$ `out` and $D2$: `pzn` $\to$ `out`, we need a way to get current back to the piezo.
        The FBR is the safest way.

    *   *One more idea:* A "Charge Pump" using the SYNC switches.
        $S1$: `pzp` to `n1`
        $S2$: `n1` to `out`
        But the SYNC controllers are tied to the piezo peaks.
        Let's stick to the SSHI.

    *   *Wait, I should check the Zener again.*
        $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$.
        `DZ33` breakdown is 3.3 V.
        If I put `DZ33` from `0` to `out`, it will clamp $V_{out}$ to $\sim 3.3\text{ V}$.
        This fits the $1.8 \le V \le 3.6$ range.
